title: India May Open Its ₹17 Lakh Crore Pension System to NRIs and OCIs
excerpt: Draft FEMA rules would let overseas Indians invest in the National Pension System with fully repatriable benefits, as part of a broader push to attract foreign capital.
body:
• Draft FEMA (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2026 would formally allow NRIs and OCIs to subscribe to India's National Pension System, with fully repatriable annuity and accumulated savings.
  • The NPS currently manages ₹17.27 lakh crore in assets across nearly 10 crore subscribers, but has had limited formal access for overseas Indians.
  • The pension reform is part of a broader package of foreign capital measures, including expanded access to listed equities and new RBI hedging support for bank deposits.
  • PFRDA has simultaneously opened on-tap licensing for new pension fund managers, signaling a wider expansion of the system.

India's government is preparing to formally open its massive National Pension System to Non-Resident Indians and Overseas Citizens of India, a move that could give millions of diaspora members a regulated, government-backed retirement savings vehicle with full repatriation rights.

The provision is embedded in the Draft Foreign Exchange Management (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2026, which were released for public comment this month. Under the proposed language, "a person resident outside India, being an NRI or an OCI, may subscribe to the NPS governed and administered by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority. The annuity or accumulated savings will be repatriable," according to the draft rules reviewed by The Hindu Business Line.

A Strategic Shift in Foreign Capital Policy

The pension opening doesn't exist in isolation. It is one component of a broader package of reforms aimed at attracting long-term foreign capital into India amid pressure on the rupee from rising crude oil prices, foreign portfolio investor outflows, and the ongoing West Asia conflict.

"Allowing NRIs and OCIs to invest in the NPS with repatriable benefits is a strategic move to encourage long-term participation by overseas Indians in India's financial markets and attract stable foreign capital rather than short-term flows."

— Akshat Khetan, Founder, AU Corporate Advisory & Legal Services

Other measures in the draft package include expanding the list of specified securities under the Fully Accessible Route for foreign investment, increasing investment limits for NRIs and OCIs in listed equities, and having the Reserve Bank of India bear the full hedging cost for banks raising fresh three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits.

What the NPS Offers — and What Changes for NRIs

The NPS is a market-linked, government-regulated retirement savings scheme managed by PFRDA. As of June 2026, assets under management stood at ₹17.27 lakh crore, with state government employees accounting for 51 per cent of the corpus, followed by central government employees at 25 per cent, the corporate sector at 17 per cent, and the all-citizens category at 5 per cent.

While NRIs have technically been able to contribute to NPS through NRE and NRO accounts, the regulatory framework has been ambiguous, and OCIs have faced additional hurdles around account transitions and repatriability. The draft FEMA rules would codify access and, crucially, guarantee that both annuity income and lump-sum withdrawals are fully repatriable — a significant improvement for overseas Indians who need to move retirement funds across borders.

Separately, PFRDA announced on July 16 that it has opened an on-tap registration window for new pension fund managers, replacing the previous system of periodic application windows. Eligible fund managers must have at least five years of experience in equity and debt management, a net worth of at least ₹50 crore, and paid-up capital of ₹25 crore. Together with the Atal Pension Yojana, the NPS now has over 9.95 crore subscribers.

What Overseas Indians Should Watch For

The draft rules are not yet final. They are open for public comment, and the specifics — including any caps on contributions, tax treaty implications, and operational procedures for account opening from abroad — will be worked out during the finalization process. NRIs considering NPS investments will also need to weigh the scheme's lock-in structure: withdrawals are restricted until age 60, with limited partial withdrawal allowed after 3 years for specific purposes like medical emergencies or children's education.

For the Indian government, the calculus is straightforward. Diaspora remittances already top $120 billion annually, making India the world's largest recipient. Converting even a fraction of that flow into long-term pension assets would deepen India's capital markets while offering NRIs a structured retirement pathway tied to their home country.
